The first thing that comes is the quiet hum of possibility, like a wire stretched between two uncertain poles. A thousand words feel both infinite and impossibly small. I could tell you about the way rain sounds different on different roofs—how it drums on corrugated tin like impatient fingers, how it whispers against slate like someone trying not to wake the house. Or I could tell you about the particular shade of loneliness that arrives at 3:17 a.m. when even the internet has gone to sleep and you're left with only the blue glow of a screen and the knowledge that everyone you love is dreaming without you.

But maybe that's too easy. Maybe what comes next is the memory of my grandmother's hands—how they looked like crumpled maps after eighty years of folding laundry, kneading dough, and pointing out constellations she could no longer see. She used to say that time doesn't pass, it accumulates. That we're all just walking museums of our own small disasters and quiet victories. I think about that often now, how every scar is a story we chose to keep wearing on the outside.

There's a bird outside my window right now making a sound I've never heard before. It isn't singing so much as arguing with the morning. I respect that. Most of us have forgotten how to argue with mornings. We just let them happen to us like polite guests we didn't invite but feel obligated to entertain. The bird doesn't care. The bird has opinions about dawn and it's going to share them whether the neighborhood likes it or not.

I wonder
